topic: How did OneCoin convince millions to invest in a cryptocurrency that was not real?

angles.angle: OneCoin took in more than $4 billion, yet prosecutors say it had no true blockchain: unlike a real coin's public ledger, its records were private and its bosses handed out coins that existed nowhere.
angles.visual: A ledger page copies itself onto a wall of devices; for OneCoin the wall goes dark and one locked notebook is left, typed into by hand.

angles.angle: Millions of ordinary people bought in worldwide between 2014 and 2016 [VERIFY: victim count].
angles.visual: Dots of light spreading across a paper map.

angles.angle: Dr Ruja Ignatova, the polished 'Cryptoqueen', filled Wembley Arena in 2016 and sold OneCoin on stage as the bitcoin killer: the credibility was the product.
angles.visual: Arena spotlights sweep and lock on an empty podium while thousands of phone lights rise.

angles.angle: In October 2017 Ruja boarded a flight from Sofia to Athens and was never seen again; in 2022 the FBI put her on its Ten Most Wanted list.
angles.visual: A boarding pass tears in two as a flight line draws and its radar blip fades over the sea.

angles.angle: Buyers paid for coin packages and earned commissions for recruiting others: belief spread because every believer was paid to recruit the next one.
angles.visual: A recruitment tree grows downward while money climbs every branch to one crown.

angles.angle: Co-founder Sebastian Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison while the founder never faced a courtroom.
The coin's price was set by the company, not a market, and only ever went up [VERIFY].
angles.visual: A hand draws a price line that never dips.

angles.angle: Victims can claim from about $40 million in forfeited assets, a sliver of what was lost [VERIFY].
angles.visual: A huge stack beside a thin coin.
